Within the last quarter century, the extant definition delineated by the Iron Curtain has become rather obsolete: the Baltic states and Bohemia are now comparable to Greece or Portugal as regards wealth, and most of the countries less Yugoslavia have been amalgamated to the European Union. Thus this definition, though once reflective of political reality, must apparently be dispensed for another.

Another alternative, that of Huntington in his Clash of Civilisations, was defined by the Schism between the Greek and Roman churches, thus dividing a line from Kronstadt to Trieste. Though this is based upon a more robust system than twentieth century politics, I find another difficulty inasmuch that various countries and regions, whether Eastern or Western, increasingly drift away from Christianity altogether. Alas this would render this division similarly historical and not present. (Huntington's system also contains other oddities, such as an independent Japanese civilisation, but I digress.)

Linguistics potentially offers another answer, albeit a strained one: western Europe includes those countries with Germanic or Western Romance languages, to remove the Slavs and other groups. The awkward corridor along the Danube that separates the Yugoslavs from northern Slavs, including even a Romance language, makes this difficult to justify, as well as the fact that language itself is not apparently so decisive to civilisation. Greece's position is also awkward.

With these three alternatives apparently exhausted, with none completely satisfactory, I am curious to hear your opinion of where Europe may best be bisected.

I prefer the historical pre-bloc delineation of Western, Central and Eastern Europe. Germany, Austria, Hungary, Poland, Czechia and a few smaller appendices of the Danubian Monarchy used to form a culture area that was distinct from both the West and the East, defined by the German language as lingua franca and fealty to either the old Emperor (Austria) or the new Emperor (Prussia).

This also neatly fits well with the division set by the Greek Schism; it merely rather partitions Central from Eastern Europe in place of Western.

Indeed, the temporary disappearance of Central Europe in the Cold War might even be considered an extension of this system, as the distinction between conceptions of life based on French Enlightenment ideals and the Russian adaptation of Marxism had concealed the earlier culture of middle Europe: as Russian influence shrank from 1989, the more ancient division again becomes visible again.

The alphabetic distinction correlates intimately with the religious: as literacy spread with the Cross, the church to which either nation belonged matched the alphabet they used. Thus the Orthodox countries use variations of the Russian alphabet (except Roumania, which consciously replaced it with Latin in a wave of Francophilia in the nineteenth century).

One could even conceivably use the German treble system if one considers the Gothic letters distinct from the Roman: their historical spread included not only Germany but also Scandinavia, Bohemia and the Baltic, though not Poland or Hungary.

The Blackletter / Fraktur (and related) letters the Germans used up to 1942 are still Roman: although they're not always easy to read, they are the same letters of the Roman alphabet. The Cyrillic alphabet has different letters, many of which are more based on the Greek alphabet (although many other overlap with the Roman).

Though derived from the Roman alphabet, we have thought of the Fraktur not as a variation of the Latin, but a native German alphabet. For several decades, there was an outstanding controversy concerning which of the scripts ought to be used; Otto von Bismarck emphatically refused to read any book printed in Roman type. English speaking works, even those concerned with language, also thought of the Gothic letters as distinct from the Roman.

Both alphabets were derived from that of the Etruscans; the standard Greek alphabet meanwhile was used as the foundation of the Russian alphabet, though the similarity is less visible due to innovations for Slavonic sounds unknown to Greek and two reforms to purge the alphabet of unnecessary letters.

I know that the German type was often considered to be a separate alphabet, but I think this is an erroneous view even if Bismarck held it: it is the same ABCDEFG... row and the letters are not that hard to identify (the lower case k being arguably the most cryptic one). The distinction is one of style not symbols. Even for the Sz/Ss sign there is a non-fraktur counterpart although I wouldn't lnow if that is a modern 'reconstruction'.
